overview.title: Customizing fit() with JAX: compute_loss_and_updates() and a stateless train_step
overview.section: 7.4 Writing your own training and evaluation loops
overview.subsection: 7.4.4 Using fit() with a custom training loop
overview.main_topic: The JAX version of overriding train_step(): a compute_loss_and_updates() method built on self.stateless_call(), and a train_step(self, state, data) that unpacks the state tuple and uses jax.value_and_grad with has_aux=True.
overview.central_idea: Under JAX, Keras calls train_step with an explicit state tuple (trainable, non-trainable, optimizer and metrics variables) and expects new state back. The loss function must be a pure method returning both the loss and updated non-trainable variables, so jax.value_and_grad(..., has_aux=True) can differentiate it.
overview.importance: It shows that the stateless JAX training step from 7.4.2 fits into fit() with the same structure, and it reveals the different train_step signature JAX requires. It also flags a simplification (no moving average of the loss) that 7.4.5 later resolves.

summary:
The last backend for *Customizing fit()* is **JAX**. As in the from-scratch JAX step of section 7.4.2, you first need a function that returns the loss, but now it is a **method** of `CustomModel`: `compute_loss_and_updates(self, trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, targets, training=False)`. It runs the forward pass with **`self.stateless_call(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, training=training)`**, which returns the predictions together with updated non-trainable variables, computes `loss_fn(targets, predictions)`, and returns **both** the loss and the non-trainable variables (callout).

The authors then point out a simplification: unlike the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions, this one does **not compute a moving average of the loss**; it returns the per-batch loss value, which is less useful. Including a stateless loss tracker would make the code very verbose, and metric management is the topic of the next section (7.4.5).

The page then begins the **JAX `train_step(self, state, data)`**. Note the extra `state` argument: under JAX, Keras passes all variables explicitly. The state is unpacked into `trainable_variables`, `non_trainable_variables`, `optimizer_variables` and `metrics_variables` (callout: metrics_variables are part of it, although we won't use them here), and `data` into `inputs, targets`. A gradient function is created with **`jax.value_and_grad(self.compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True)`**, and calling it as `(loss, non_trainable_variables), grads = grad_fn(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, ...` computes the loss, the gradients with respect to the first argument (the trainable variables), and the updated non-trainable variables. The call continues on p.250, where the optimizer update and the returned `(logs, state)` appear.

concepts.name: model.stateless_call()
concepts.definition: A forward pass that takes trainable and non-trainable variables explicitly and returns outputs plus updated non-trainable variables.
concepts.intuition: Using the model as a pure function of its weights.
concepts.technical: predictions, non_trainable_variables = self.stateless_call(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, training=training)
concepts.significance: Required so JAX can differentiate the loss with respect to weights passed as arguments.
concepts.misconception: That it modifies the model's stored variables; it does not.

concepts.name: jax.value_and_grad with has_aux
concepts.definition: A JAX transformation turning f into a function that returns f's value and its gradient with respect to the first argument; with has_aux=True, f returns (value, aux).
concepts.intuition: Ask JAX for the loss and its slope in one go, and let it carry some extra baggage along.
concepts.technical: grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(self.compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True); (loss, ntv), grads = grad_fn(tv, ntv, inputs, targets, training=True)
concepts.significance: One call gives the loss for logging, the gradients for the optimizer, and the updated non-trainable state.
concepts.misconception: That gradients are taken with respect to all arguments; by default only the first (argnums=0).

code.title: JAX CustomModel: compute_loss_and_updates()
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def compute_loss_and_updates(
        self,
        trainable_variables,
        non_trainable_variables,
        inputs,
        targets,
        training=False,
    ):
        predictions, non_trainable_variables = self.stateless_call(
            trainable_variables,
            non_trainable_variables,
            inputs,
            training=training,
        )
        loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
        return loss, non_trainable_variables
code.what_it_does: Defines a pure loss method on CustomModel that runs a stateless forward pass and returns the loss plus updated non-trainable variables. The class continues with train_step in the next code block.

deeper.title: Why fit() passes state to a JAX train_step
deeper.body: Beyond the book: for TensorFlow and PyTorch, Keras variables are mutable objects that a step can update in place. For JAX, `fit()` compiles your `train_step` with `jax.jit`, so it must be pure. Keras therefore extracts all variable values into the `state` tuple, calls your compiled step, and after each step (or at the end) writes the returned values back into the model's variables. That is why you must return `state` even if you changed only part of it.

deeper.title: Signature comparison across backends
deeper.body:
| Backend | Signature | Returns | Gradient mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| TensorFlow (p.247) | `train_step(self, data)` | logs | `tf.GradientTape` |
| PyTorch (p.248) | `train_step(self, data)` | logs | `loss.backward()` |
| JAX (p.249-250) | `train_step(self, state, data)` | `(logs, state)` | `jax.value_and_grad` |

Editorial summary of the three versions.

questions.question: What does the JAX train_step receive that the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions do not?
questions.explanation: train_step(self, state, data). The loss function is a global in all versions; GradientTape is TensorFlow; the optimizer is accessed as self.optimizer.

questions.question: List the four components of the state tuple.
questions.explanation: Unpacked at the start of train_step; metrics_variables are unused here.

questions.question: Why is has_aux=True needed when building grad_fn?
questions.answer: Because compute_loss_and_updates returns a pair (loss, non_trainable_variables); has_aux tells JAX to differentiate only the first element and pass the second through as auxiliary output.
questions.explanation: Without it, JAX would expect a scalar output.

questions.question: Why does compute_loss_and_updates() return the non-trainable variables?
questions.answer: Because the forward pass may update them (e.g. normalization statistics), and in a stateless function updates must be returned rather than written in place.
questions.explanation: Callout: returns both the loss and the updated non-trainable variables; see p.242 on JAX statelessness.

questions.question: Why does this JAX example not report a moving average of the loss?
options: To simplify metric state management; including it would make the code very verbose
Because the loss is already averaged by the optimizer
Because fit() averages it automatically for JAX
questions.answer: To simplify metric state management; including it would make the code very verbose
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. JAX can compute averages; optimizers don't average losses; fit() doesn't average returned per-batch values for you.

questions.question: With respect to which argument does grad_fn compute grads, and what is the output structure?
questions.answer: With respect to trainable_variables (first argument); output is ((loss, non_trainable_variables), grads).
questions.explanation: value_and_grad defaults to argnums=0; has_aux nests the aux value with the loss.

questions.question: Can you sketch, before reading p.250, what the rest of the train_step must do?
questions.answer: Finish the grad_fn call (targets, training=True), apply the gradients with self.optimizer.stateless_apply to get new trainable and optimizer variables, then return logs and the repacked state.
